phrases.translation: Ṭâ-Sĩn. These are the verses of the Quran; the clear Book
phrases.explanation: The chapter opens with mysterious letters. The commentary records an interpretation that treats them as an oath and a divine name, while noting that such letters have been discussed earlier. What follows is then identified as the verses of the Quran and a clear Book, meaning that reflection shows the recitation comes from Allah rather than the Prophet's invention. Its clarity lies in making its divine origin recognizable, since no created being can produce its like.

phrases.translation: ˹It is˺ a guide and good news for the believers
phrases.explanation: The Quran is described as guidance and good news specifically for those who believe. Guidance means that Allah has made plain the way to truth and the path to peace, so the recitation is not merely information but a direction for life. The good news is the tremendous victory awaiting those who affirm what it contains. The commentary also notes two acceptable Arabic readings of the phrase, both yielding the same basic claim that guidance and glad tidings belong to the believers.

phrases.translation: ˹those˺ who establish prayer, pay alms-tax
phrases.explanation: The believers are first described by worship and charity. Establishing prayer means keeping the prayer with its prescribed ordinances, while paying alms-tax means giving the obligatory due. The commentary also records an interpretation in which the giving of alms is linked to purification from the defilement of disobedience. The two practices are therefore not isolated rituals. They join devotion to Allah with a concern for purity and for the obligations owed to others.

phrases.translation: and have sure faith in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The final mark of these believers is certainty about the life after death. They know that after death they will return to Allah, so they obey Him in hope of His abundant reward and in fear of His severe punishment. This separates them from those who deny resurrection and see no consequence in either good or evil. The promise of guidance and good news in the previous verse is therefore for people whose belief shapes both worship and moral conduct.

phrases.translation: As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The phrase identifies people who reject the Hereafter in its full sense. Their denial includes the resurrection, the Hour, the return to Allah after death, and the reward and punishment that follow. The commentary treats this unbelief as the root of what comes next, because a person who expects no final accounting has lost the clearest reason to distinguish right from wrong. It is a description of a settled outlook, not a momentary doubt about one detail of the unseen.

phrases.translation: We have certainly made their ˹evil˺ deeds appealing to them, so they wander blindly
phrases.explanation: Allah says He has made the ugliness of such people's deeds beloved and easy for them. As a result they wander bewildered in the misguidance of those deeds, all the while supposing that they are doing good. The phrase does not say that the deeds have become good, only that the people's judgment of them has been distorted. Their blindness is therefore moral before it is intellectual. They no longer recognize the harm they are choosing.

phrases.translation: It is they who will suffer a dreadful torment
phrases.explanation: The worst punishment is promised to the same people who reject the Hereafter. The commentary says this punishment begins in the present world and identifies it historically with the polytheists of Quraysh who were killed at Badr. That identification belongs to the first audience of the verse, but the principle is broader. A life built on denying accountability already carries a severe penalty before the final judgment arrives.

phrases.translation: and in the Hereafter they will ˹truly˺ be the greatest losers
phrases.explanation: In the Hereafter their loss is described in the language of trade. Their merchandise is the least profitable because they purchased error in exchange for right guidance. The image makes their choice look like a bargain in which they gave away the only thing of lasting value. They are the greatest losers not because they lacked opportunity, but because they traded guidance away and then found that their transaction brought no profit at all.

phrases.translation: And indeed, you ˹O Prophet˺ are receiving the Quran from the One ˹Who is˺ All-Wise, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told that he receives, preserves, and learns the Quran from One who is All-Wise and All-Knowing. Wisdom here refers to Allah's governance of creation, while knowledge includes the affairs of His creatures, their interests, their past history, and what will happen to them. The phrase therefore answers any suspicion that the recitation is the Prophet's own composition. Its source is the One whose wisdom and knowledge encompass everything the revelation addresses.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when Moses said to his family, “I have spotted a fire
phrases.explanation: Moses is on a journey from Madyan to Egypt with his household when night cold overtakes them and his flint fails to produce fire. Seeing or perceiving a fire, he tells his family to remain where they are. The commentary connects this moment with Allah's knowledge in the previous verse, since the One sending the Quran knows this earlier incident. What looks like an ordinary search for warmth becomes the beginning of a divine encounter.

phrases.translation: I will either bring you some directions from there, or a burning torch so you may warm yourselves
phrases.explanation: Moses expects to bring either news of the fire or a burning brand taken from it so his family can warm themselves. The commentary discusses two well-known Arabic readings of the word for the flame, one understanding it as fire kindled from the source and the other as a lit torch. It regards both readings as sound and close in meaning. The practical point is unchanged, since Moses hopes for guidance to the fire and warmth from it.

phrases.translation: But when he came to it, he was called ˹by Allah˺, “Blessed is the one at the fire, and whoever is around it
phrases.explanation: When Moses reaches the fire, a call declares blessing on the one at the fire and those around it. The commentary preserves several interpretations. Some understand the fire as Allah's light or a place of His call, others say the fire itself is blessed, and others identify those around it as angels, or Moses and the angels together. The phrase therefore marks the site as sacred without settling every detail of how the blessing is to be understood.

phrases.translation: Glory be to Allah, the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The call ends by declaring that all sanctity belongs to Allah, the Lord of all worlds, who is far above what wrongdoers ascribe to Him. The verse moves from a mysterious blessing at the fire to an explicit affirmation of divine transcendence. Moses is not being invited to worship the fire or the light. He is being prepared to hear the voice of the One who owns and governs every world.

phrases.translation: O Moses! It is truly I. I am Allah—the Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The call now identifies the speaker directly. The wording stresses that it is truly Allah who addresses Moses, and the following names explain what that means. He is Almighty in His retribution against His enemies and All-Wise in His direction of creation. The commentary also discusses an unusual pronoun in the Arabic sentence, but its role is to reinforce the certainty of the statement. The One speaking from the fire is none other than the sovereign Lord.

phrases.translation: Now, throw down your staff!” But when he saw it slithering like a snake, he ran away without looking back
phrases.explanation: At the command to throw down his staff, an omitted step is understood, since the staff becomes a moving serpent. Moses sees it and flees in fear, turning away without returning or looking back. The commentary explains the serpent as a known kind of large snake. The sign is real enough to frighten him, and his reaction is presented as a natural human response before Allah gives him the reassurance that follows.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah reassured him,˺ “O Moses! Do not be afraid! Messengers should have no fear in My presence
phrases.explanation: Allah tells Moses not to fear, because messengers who stand in His presence have no reason to be afraid. The commentary explains that prophets favored with revelation are granted security, while also discussing an exception for wrongdoing and one report that connects Moses' fear to an earlier killing. It further reports that he only became calm when the staff was restored to its normal state. The reassurance therefore addresses both the sign and the fear it produced.

phrases.translation: ˹Fear is˺ only for those who do wrong
phrases.explanation: The previous promise of safety for messengers is qualified. Fear belongs to one who has done wrong, not to prophethood as such. The commentary records a grammatical debate about how the exception works, but prefers the view that a servant who has sinned has reason to fear Allah's punishment. One report connects Moses' fear to an earlier killing. The phrase therefore treats fear as the result of wrongdoing, while making clear that the messengers are otherwise secure in Allah's presence.

phrases.translation: But if they later mend ˹their˺ evil ˹ways˺ with good, then I am certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The verse then opens a new statement about repentance. Whoever has done wrong but afterwards replaces evil with good is promised forgiveness and mercy. The commentary explains this as turning back from sin, after which Allah conceals the wrong and refrains from punishing it. The promise is broad enough to include messengers and other creatures. It does not erase the earlier warning about fear, but shows the way out of it through sincere change and divine compassion.

phrases.translation: Now put your hand through ˹the opening of˺ your collar, it will come out ˹shining˺ white, unblemished
phrases.explanation: Moses is told to place his palm inside the neck opening of his garment, which was a woolen mantle with no sleeve or only a short one. His hand will come out radiantly white, but not with the whiteness of disease, since the commentary explicitly denies leprosy. The transformation is a miracle rather than an illness. Like the staff, it becomes a visible sign that the One who commands it can alter ordinary reality.

phrases.translation: ˹These are two˺ of nine signs for Pharaoh and his people
phrases.explanation: The shining hand joins the staff among the nine signs given to Moses for Pharaoh and his people. The commentary understands these as the proofs mentioned elsewhere in the Quran, including the staff, the hand, locusts, lice, frogs, the flood, blood, the stone, and an affliction on property. Together they form a sustained argument, not isolated wonders. Each sign calls the same people to acknowledge the truth of Moses' message.

phrases.translation: They have truly been a rebellious people
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh and his people are called rebellious because they were ungrateful and unbelieving toward Allah. The commentary explains the word as moral corruption that issues in disbelief, not merely political disobedience. The description gives the reason the signs were sent. They came to a people already committed to rejecting their Lord, so the wonders would test their response rather than simply entertain them.

phrases.translation: But when Our enlightening signs came to them, they said, “This is pure magic
phrases.explanation: The signs given to Pharaoh are described as enlightening because they were proofs and arguments for the truth of Moses' message, clear to anyone who beheld them. Yet the people respond by calling them manifest sorcery. The commentary says they claimed the works made their magical character obvious to onlookers. The verse therefore exposes a contradiction. What was sent to clarify the truth was deliberately relabelled as deception by those unwilling to accept it.

phrases.translation: And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly
phrases.explanation: The denial of Pharaoh's people is especially serious because their hearts were certain the signs came from Allah. They did not reject them from lack of evidence. The commentary explains their refusal as injustice, presumption, and haughtiness after the truth had become clear. Their knowledge increased their responsibility rather than saving them. The phrase warns that certainty in the mind can still be resisted when pride and self-interest govern the will.

phrases.translation: See then what was the end of the corruptors
phrases.explanation: Allah tells the Prophet to look with the eye of the heart at what became of those who denied clear signs. The commentary recalls their loss of gardens, springs, crops, and honorable homes, then drowning in this life and lasting punishment in the next. The command is not merely to remember a past event. It establishes a pattern for how Allah deals with those who reject the truth after it has been made plain.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We granted knowledge to David and Solomon. And they said ˹in acknowledgment˺
phrases.explanation: Allah gave David and Solomon special knowledge, including the language of birds and animals and other gifts He singled out for them. Their immediate response is acknowledgement and praise rather than pride in their own ability. The phrase introduces the saying that follows, so the reader understands their words as gratitude for a gift. Knowledge is treated as something received, and the proper first response to it is to recognize the Giver.

phrases.translation: All praise is for Allah Who has privileged us over many of His faithful servants
phrases.explanation: David and Solomon praise Allah for favoring them above many believing servants of their own time. The commentary stresses the word many, so the claim is not a comparison with every believer of every age. What matters is that the privilege is attributed entirely to Allah. Their gratitude turns distinction into worship, acknowledging that any advantage they possess came from His choice and not from their own superiority.

phrases.translation: And David was succeeded by Solomon, who said, “O people
phrases.explanation: Solomon inherits from David the knowledge and kingship Allah had given him, not merely private property. The commentary says this authority was assigned to Solomon above his father's other sons and above the people of his nation. Addressing the people, he announces what Allah has taught him. The succession is therefore part of a divine gift, and Solomon's first public words are an acknowledgment of what he has received.

phrases.translation: We have been taught the language of birds, and been given everything ˹we need˺. This is indeed a great privilege
phrases.explanation: Solomon says he has been taught the speech of birds, meaning that he understands what they say, just as a person understands human speech. He has also been given of every good, including the knowledge and authority described around him. The commentary calls this a manifest privilege above his contemporaries, clear to anyone who reflects on it. The point is not literal possession of every existing thing but an extraordinary share of divine favor.

phrases.translation: Solomon’s forces of jinn, humans, and birds were rallied for him, perfectly organized
phrases.explanation: Solomon's armies of jinn, humans, and birds are gathered and arranged in ordered ranks. The commentary records different explanations of the final word. Some say the front is held back until the rear catches up, others say the troops are driven forward, and others that they race ahead. It prefers the first, because the Arabic term can mean restraint. The picture is of a vast, diverse host under disciplined control.

phrases.translation: And when they came across a valley of ants, an ant warned, “O ants
phrases.explanation: Solomon and his armies reach a valley associated with ants, and a single ant addresses the rest. The wording gives the tiny creature speech and communal concern, which fits Solomon's gift of understanding the language of birds and other creatures. The commentary does not linger on the marvel of the speech itself. It treats the warning as the point, since the ant recognizes a danger that the approaching army has not noticed.

phrases.translation: Go quickly into your homes so Solomon and his armies do not crush you, unknowingly
phrases.explanation: The ant tells the others to enter their homes so Solomon and his soldiers do not crush them without knowing it. The commentary makes the danger explicit, saying the army could kill them while unaware of what it had done. The warning is not an accusation of deliberate cruelty but a recognition of overwhelming power. Even a just ruler's army can harm the small because its attention lies elsewhere.

phrases.translation: So Solomon smiled in amusement at her words, and prayed, “My Lord
phrases.explanation: Solomon smiles and laughs at the ant's words, then turns immediately to prayer. The moment could have been only amusement at an unexpected small voice, but the response reveals his character. The commentary says he asks Allah to inspire him, using a word that can mean enable or urge. His wonder at the created world becomes an occasion for seeking help in gratitude rather than congratulating himself.

phrases.translation: Inspire me to ˹always˺ be thankful for Your favours which You have blessed me and my parents with, and to do good deeds that please you
phrases.explanation: Solomon asks to be inspired to thank Allah for favors shown to him and to his parents, and to perform deeds that please Him. The commentary explains this as acting in accordance with obedience, so thanksgiving is not limited to words. He wants gratitude to shape his conduct. The mention of his parents places his own gifts within a family history of divine kindness, widening the circle of what he must acknowledge.

phrases.translation: Admit me, by Your mercy, into ˹the company of˺ Your righteous servants
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends by asking Allah, through His mercy, to place Solomon among His righteous servants. The commentary understands these servants as the prophets and believers chosen for revelation and obedience, and interprets the request as admission to Paradise where they enter. Even a prophet endowed with extraordinary knowledge therefore seeks the final goal as a gift of mercy. His privileges do not make him independent of Allah's compassion.

phrases.translation: ˹One day˺ he inspected the birds, and wondered
phrases.explanation: Solomon inspects the birds, but the commentary says the reason for the inspection is not settled. One report says he needed the hoopoe to locate water during a journey, while another says each kind of bird had a turn to attend and the hoopoe missed its turn. Since no decisive revelation identifies the cause, the commentary leaves both possibilities open. What is clear is that a missing small bird matters to a king whose rule includes the birds.

phrases.translation: Why is it that I cannot see the hoopoe? Or could he be absent
phrases.explanation: Solomon's question asks whether his gaze has missed the hoopoe even though it is present, or whether it truly belongs among the absent. The wording shows careful inspection rather than a hasty conclusion. The same uncertainty about the bird's location appears in the reports about why he looked for it. This brief question prepares the threat that follows, since Solomon must decide how to treat an unexplained absence in his ordered host.

phrases.translation: I will surely subject him to a severe punishment
phrases.explanation: Solomon swears to punish the hoopoe severely. The commentary explains the punishment through reports that describe plucking out a bird's feathers, sometimes with exposure to the sun. These details are transmitted explanations rather than a universal law about discipline. The phrase shows that the king treats absence from duty as a serious matter, but the next clause immediately leaves room for a valid explanation, so punishment is not presented as automatic.

phrases.translation: or ˹even˺ slaughter him, unless he brings me a compelling excuse
phrases.explanation: The alternative to severe punishment is slaughter, unless the hoopoe brings a clear proof that exonerates it. The commentary says that the word translated as authority here means a proof or a convincing excuse, and it notes that this meaning recurs in the Quran. Solomon is therefore asking for evidence, not mere eloquence. The bird's life depends on whether its account of why it disappeared can be shown to be true.

phrases.translation: It was not long before the bird came and said, “I have found out something you do not know
phrases.explanation: The hoopoe returns after only a short wait and claims knowledge that Solomon does not possess. The statement is bold, since it is addressed to a prophet-king endowed with extraordinary understanding. Yet the commentary explains it simply as knowledge of something outside Solomon's awareness. The verse sets up the news from Sheba as the evidence that will justify the bird's absence and turn a threatened punishment into a hearing.

phrases.translation: I have just come to you from Sheba with sure news
phrases.explanation: The bird says it has come from Sheba with certain news. The commentary records different Arabic readings of the name, variously understood as a man, a tribe, or a region, and accepts both main readings. The report is described as sure or certain because it concerns a kingdom Solomon's own dominion had not reached. The news is not rumor but information gathered by direct presence, which is why it can serve as the hoopoe's proof.

phrases.translation: Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them
phrases.explanation: The hoopoe reports a woman reigning over Sheba. The commentary says this news explains why Solomon accepts the bird's excuse, since he had not known of another earthly kingdom and now hears of a people who worship something other than Allah. The detail is therefore more than political curiosity. It presents a realm outside his rule and a religious error that calls for a response, making the bird's absence consequential.

phrases.translation: who has been given everything ˹she needs˺, and who has a magnificent throne
phrases.explanation: The queen is said to have been given everything needed by a ruler, meaning the equipment and resources of worldly kingship. Her throne is magnificent in worth and significance, not merely in physical size. The commentary preserves reports describing a noble seat made with gold and precious stones. The description prepares for the later episode of the throne, while also showing that the queen's power is real even though it remains subordinate to Allah.

phrases.translation: I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah
phrases.explanation: The hoopoe's report turns from political power to worship. The queen and her people prostrate to the sun rather than to Allah, treating a created light as an object of devotion. The commentary understands this as sun worship in place of the worship due to the Creator. The phrase identifies the central problem of Sheba, so the story is not simply about extending Solomon's kingdom but about calling people away from false worship.

phrases.translation: For Satan has made their deeds appealing to them—hindering them from the ˹Right˺ Way and leaving them unguided
phrases.explanation: Satan has made sun worship seem fair and beloved to the people of Sheba, and so has held them back from the straight path. The commentary identifies that path with the religion Allah sent through His prophets. Because their error appears attractive to them, they do not find their way to the truth and continue wandering. The verse therefore traces misguidance to a distortion of desire as well as to a wrong belief.

phrases.translation: so they do not prostrate to Allah, Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth
phrases.explanation: Two well-known readings shape this opening. One can be understood as a call to prostrate to Allah, while the other says Satan's deception kept the people from prostrating to Him. The commentary accepts both meanings. Allah is then described as the One who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, such as rain and crops. The One who discloses concealed sustenance is the One who should be worshipped.

phrases.translation: and knows what you ˹all˺ conceal and what you reveal
phrases.explanation: Allah also knows what people conceal and what they make public. The commentary says this includes the hidden and open deeds of those whose sun worship Satan made attractive, and more broadly the secrets of all creatures. The phrase completes the argument against false worship. The sun neither knows nor discloses, while Allah knows both the secret and the visible act, and therefore alone deserves the prostration that was being withheld.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him
phrases.explanation: The hoopoe's speech ends with a clear confession of monotheism. Worship is due to Allah alone, with no partner or other object of devotion set beside Him. The commentary notes that these words are still part of the bird's report, not a separate statement by Solomon. The effect is striking, since a small creature rebukes the worship of a great kingdom by naming the only true God and calling for sincere obedience.

phrases.translation: the Lord of the Mighty Throne
phrases.explanation: Allah is called Lord of the Mighty Throne, meaning the Owner of a throne to which every other throne is subordinate. The commentary explicitly contrasts it with the magnificent throne of the queen of Sheba. No earthly seat, however splendid, can equal His dominion. The phrase therefore puts the queen's power in perspective and prepares for the later test in which her own throne becomes a sign.

phrases.translation: Solomon said, “We will see whether you are telling the truth or lying
phrases.explanation: Solomon does not immediately accept or reject the hoopoe's report. He says he will examine the excuse and proof the bird has brought, along with the news itself, to determine whether it is true or false. The commentary explains the verb as investigation rather than simple seeing. The response is cautious and just, since the threatened punishment depended on whether the bird's account could be verified.

phrases.translation: Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them
phrases.explanation: Solomon gives the hoopoe a letter to deliver to the people of Sheba. The commentary includes reports about how the bird reached the queen, including entering by a window and placing the letter before her. The command turns the bird from a bearer of news into a messenger. Solomon is testing the report by beginning a direct exchange with the distant kingdom rather than acting only on the hoopoe's word.

phrases.translation: then stand aside and see how they will respond
phrases.explanation: The order of standing aside and observing is debated. One explanation says the hoopoe should deliver the letter, see the response, and then return, while another says it should withdraw nearby and watch the queen's consultation. The commentary prefers the second because the consultation follows the letter's arrival. Either way, Solomon wants evidence of how the people receive his summons, not simply confirmation that the letter reached them.

phrases.translation: The Queen ˹later˺ announced, “O chiefs
phrases.explanation: After reading the letter, the queen addresses the chiefs or nobles of her people. The commentary describes them as her counselors and includes reports about her court and lineage, but the narrative point is the public consultation. She does not hide the letter or decide alone. A message that challenges her worship and authority is brought immediately into the council where matters of state are judged.

phrases.translation: Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me
phrases.explanation: The queen calls the letter noble. The commentary records two explanations, that it was sealed or that it came from a noble king, and it does not decisively choose between them. Both reasons make the letter worthy of attention before its contents are even considered. The phrase also shows that the queen recognizes the sender's stature, which helps explain why she seeks counsel instead of dismissing the message.

phrases.translation: It is from Solomon, and it reads
phrases.explanation: The letter is identified as coming from Solomon. The commentary notes that prophets wrote concisely and did not add lengthy formalities, so the wording reported in the Quran is the substance of the letter itself. The direct attribution matters because the call that follows is not from an anonymous adviser. It comes from a prophet-king whose authority the queen has to assess.

phrases.translation: In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The letter opens in the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. The commentary treats this invocation as part of the actual writing, not later commentary. It places the whole message under Allah's authority and mercy before any demand is made. For a people who worship the sun, the opening itself is a challenge, since the true God is named as the source of the summons.

phrases.translation: Do not be arrogant with me, but come to me, fully submitting ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The message forbids the queen and her people from exalting themselves above Solomon and commands them to come in submission. The commentary explains the first clause as refusing to behave arrogantly toward the call, and the second as coming obediently submissive to Allah in His oneness and obedience. The demand is therefore religious before it is political. Solomon wants their worship corrected, not merely their formal surrender.

phrases.translation: She said, “O chiefs! Advise me in this matter of mine
phrases.explanation: The queen asks her nobles for a considered answer about the matter that has come upon her. The commentary says she treats the consultation almost like a legal verdict concerning the sender of the letter. She recognizes that the message requires a decision about both power and religion. Her question invites the chiefs to assess the threat together, rather than allowing fear or pride to dictate a private response.

phrases.translation: for I would never make any decision without you
phrases.explanation: The queen says she would not settle any matter before her counsellors were present. The commentary explains this as her regular practice of consultation, not a momentary weakness. The statement gives the nobles real responsibility for the answer they will give, while also showing her political skill. She keeps authority in her own hands but refuses to bypass the people whose military support she would need.

phrases.translation: They responded, “We are a people of strength and great ˹military˺ might
phrases.explanation: The chiefs answer by stressing their capacity for combat and fierce valor in war. The commentary includes reports of very large forces under their command, though the narrative needs only the claim of strength. They offer the queen the option of resistance. Their answer acknowledges the military dimension of Solomon's letter, since a refusal to submit could lead to confrontation with a powerful outside ruler.

phrases.translation: but the decision is yours, so decide what you will command
phrases.explanation: Despite their confidence, the chiefs leave the final decision to the queen. The commentary says they place the choice between fighting and refraining in her hands and promise obedience to whatever she commands. Their deference shows that military strength is not the same as political authority. The narrative now turns to the queen's judgment, which will test whether she uses that strength wisely.

phrases.translation: She reasoned, “Indeed, when kings invade a land
phrases.explanation: The queen responds by describing what conquerors normally do when they enter a settlement by force. The commentary specifies that she is speaking of kings who invade with superior power, not every ruler who visits peacefully. Her words are practical political reasoning. She wants her counsellors to understand that war with Solomon could bring devastation rather than the glory their offer of battle might suggest.

phrases.translation: they ruin it and debase its nobles. They really do so
phrases.explanation: The queen says invading kings ruin a land and turn its honored people into the debased. The commentary explains this devastation as laying waste and enslaving free people. Allah then confirms that this is indeed how such conquerors act. Her argument therefore carries divine endorsement. It is not an exaggerated fear but an accurate description of the violence that forced conquest brings upon a community.

phrases.translation: But I will certainly send him a gift
phrases.explanation: The queen decides to send a gift as a test. The commentary reports that she wanted to know whether Solomon was a worldly king or a prophet, since a king might accept wealth while a prophet would refuse it and demand a change of religion. Reports describe disguised servants and valuable presents, but their purpose is the same. The gift is a diplomatic probe, not simple generosity.

phrases.translation: and see what ˹response˺ my envoys will return with
phrases.explanation: The queen waits to see what her envoys bring back, whether acceptance of the gift and withdrawal, or its rejection and persistence in the religious summons. The commentary explains that she is looking for both a report and a sign of how Solomon treats worldly wealth. Her plan is cautious. Before risking war or surrender, she tries to discover what kind of authority she is dealing with.

phrases.translation: When the chief-envoy came to him, Solomon said, “Do you offer me wealth
phrases.explanation: The envoy arrives with the queen's gift, and Solomon asks whether they mean to assist him with wealth. The commentary discusses singular and plural wording for the messenger and notes accepted Arabic readings of the verb, but the sense is plain. The gift is being offered as a means of influence. Solomon's question exposes that purpose rather than treating the present as a gesture of friendship.

phrases.translation: What Allah has granted me is far greater than what He has granted you. No! It is you who rejoice in ˹receiving˺ gifts
phrases.explanation: Solomon replies that what Allah has given him is better and greater than what the queen's people possess. The commentary says this includes wealth, power, and authority unlike that granted to others. He does not rejoice in the gift, while they rejoice in such things because they treat worldly abundance as glory and compete in it. The rejection shows that his aim cannot be bought.

phrases.translation: Go back to them, for we will certainly mobilize against them forces which they can never resist
phrases.explanation: Solomon tells the envoy to return with the gift and warns that he will bring forces the people of Sheba cannot withstand. The commentary explains that they would have no capacity to resist or repel those armies. The warning follows the rejection of wealth and makes clear that the issue is not tribute. It is submission to Allah, and the military threat is conditional on their refusal.

phrases.translation: and we will drive them out from there in disgrace, fully humbled
phrases.explanation: The warning continues that the people will be driven from their land in humiliation and lowliness. The commentary says this would happen if they did not come to Solomon in submission to Allah. The phrase reverses the queen's earlier fear about conquering kings, since she had described exactly such devastation. Her choice is now between accepting the call peacefully and suffering the outcome she herself understood.

phrases.translation: Solomon asked, “O chiefs
phrases.explanation: Solomon addresses the chiefs among his jinn and human followers, asking which of them can bring the queen's throne. The timing of this question is disputed. Some place it immediately after the hoopoe's report as a test of the bird's truthfulness, while others place it after the queen's envoys have left and she is on her way. The narrative does not settle the order, but the request turns the distant throne into the next sign.

phrases.translation: Which of you can bring me her throne before they come to me in ˹full˺ submission
phrases.explanation: The commentators offer several reasons Solomon wants the throne before the people arrive in submission. Some say he feared her property would become protected once she accepted faith, others that he wanted to test her intelligence, and the preferred explanation is that the throne would prove his prophethood and Allah's power. The phrase about submission is understood as willing obedience, since the queen had not yet embraced faith when she arrived.

phrases.translation: One mighty jinn responded, “I can bring it to you before you rise from this council of yours
phrases.explanation: A mighty jinn, described as rebellious or shrewd, volunteers to bring the throne before Solomon rises from the seat where he judges. Reports say he sat until midday, so the offer is swift but still bounded by a human interval. The jinn claims both strength and trustworthiness, meaning he can carry the throne and will not betray the precious things in it. His confidence is real, yet the next speaker will surpass it.

phrases.translation: And I am quite strong and trustworthy for this ˹task˺
phrases.explanation: The jinn's promise of strength and trust is a claim about ability and honesty. The commentary explains that he would be strong enough to carry the throne and trustworthy with its valuables, and one report extends the trust to the queen herself. The offer shows that Solomon's command reaches powerful nonhuman servants, but the narrative immediately introduces someone with a different kind of power. Knowledge of the Book will accomplish more than brute strength.

phrases.translation: But the one who had knowledge of the Scripture said, “I can bring it to you in the blink of an eye
phrases.explanation: A human being with knowledge from the Book says he can bring the throne before Solomon's glance returns. Reports differ about his name and about the exact sense of the glance, whether it reaches its farthest point or returns from it, but they agree on extraordinary speed. The commentary links his knowledge to a divine name by which Allah answers prayer. The throne then rises from beneath the earth and appears before Solomon.

phrases.translation: So when Solomon saw it placed before him, he exclaimed, “This is by the grace of my Lord to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful
phrases.explanation: Seeing the throne settled before him, Solomon calls it a favor from his Lord and a test of whether he will be grateful or ungrateful. The commentary says the test concerns his whole insight, power, and kingdom, not the object alone. One interpretation adds that he is being tested by seeing someone less powerful in the world possess greater knowledge. His response is therefore to turn a marvel into self-examination rather than pride.

phrases.translation: And whoever is grateful, it is only for their own good. But whoever is ungrateful, surely my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Most Generous
phrases.explanation: Solomon says gratitude benefits the grateful person alone, while Allah remains Self-Sufficient and Generous. The commentary explains that Allah does not need human thanks and gains nothing from it. Gratitude exposes the servant to benefit, and ingratitude harms only the servant. Yet Allah's generosity continues even toward those who misuse His gifts in disobedience. The verse closes the episode by placing extraordinary power within a moral test about thankfulness.

phrases.translation: ˹Then˺ Solomon said, “Disguise her throne for her so we may see whether she will recognize ˹it˺ or she will not be able to
phrases.explanation: Solomon orders the queen's throne to be disguised by adding and removing parts, so that he can see whether she recognizes it. The commentary says the purpose is to test her understanding, and reports connect the test with claims the jinn had made about her. Those reports vary, but the central point is discernment. A changed object from her own locked chamber will show whether she can perceive the truth about Solomon's message.

phrases.translation: So when she arrived, it was said ˹to her˺, “Is your throne like this
phrases.explanation: When the queen reaches Solomon, she is shown the altered throne and asked whether hers looks like it. The commentary notes that she had left her own throne behind in Sheba, so the question is a test rather than an ordinary request for identification. The wording does not directly say whose object it is. It invites her to compare what she sees with what she knows, preparing for her careful answer.

phrases.translation: She replied, “It looks to be the same
phrases.explanation: The queen replies that it looks to be the same, likening the altered throne to her own without flatly identifying it. The commentary says she was in doubt, which makes her answer prudent. She neither denies the resemblance nor claims more than she can see. Her intelligence is shown in this measured response, and the test of the throne succeeds without Solomon having to explain what he has done.

phrases.translation: We have ˹already˺ received knowledge ˹of Solomon’s prophethood˺ before this ˹miracle˺, and have submitted ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The final statement is attributed by the commentary to Solomon rather than to the queen. He says that he and his followers were given knowledge before her and were already submitted to Allah. The knowledge concerns Allah's power to do what He wills, demonstrated by bringing the throne. The phrase therefore contrasts the longstanding faith of Solomon's community with the queen's later arrival at belief, rather than describing her submission before the miracle.

phrases.translation: But she had been hindered by what she used to worship instead of Allah
phrases.explanation: The queen had been held back by what she worshipped instead of Allah, especially the sun. The commentary says this false worship and unbelief kept her from recognizing the truth and worshipping Allah. It also allows other readings in which Solomon turns her away from those objects or Allah does so by granting her faith. These possibilities share the same result, since her former religion is described as an obstacle that had to be removed.

phrases.translation: for she was indeed from a disbelieving people
phrases.explanation: The queen belonged to a disbelieving people, and the commentary says she was herself an unbeliever from that community. Her sun worship was the religion of her people and ancestors, and she followed their example. The phrase is not a general insult against a modern community. It explains why her response to Solomon was delayed, since inherited practice can make even a clear sign harder to accept.

phrases.translation: Then she was told, “Enter the palace.” But when she saw the hall, she thought it was a body of water, so she bared her legs
phrases.explanation: The queen is invited into a pavilion made of clear glass with water flowing beneath it. Thinking the floor is deep water, she uncovers her legs to wade through. The commentary gives two reasons for the construction, to display a dominion greater than hers and to test reports about her appearance, and allows that both may be true. The immediate point is that her senses are deceived by something designed to reveal Solomon's power.

phrases.translation: Solomon said. “It is just a palace paved with crystal.” ˹At last˺ she declared, “My Lord
phrases.explanation: Solomon explains that the apparent water is only a glass pavilion, not a sea. The commentary says the queen then understood that she had been overcome, and she cries out to her Lord. The correction of her mistake is part of the sign. What had seemed a danger is shown to be a structure under human control, and the recognition of that power prepares her for the confession that follows.

phrases.translation: I have certainly wronged my soul. Now I ˹fully˺ submit myself along with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: The queen confesses that she has wronged herself and submits with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds. The commentary explains the wrong as worshipping the sun and prostrating to others besides Allah. Her submission is described as obedience joined to the affirmation of His oneness, singling Him out in divinity and dominion. The story of Sheba therefore ends not merely in political surrender but in a change of worship.

phrases.translation: And We certainly sent to the people of Thamûd their brother Ṣâliḥ
phrases.explanation: Allah sent Salih as a brother from among the people of Thamud, with the command to worship Allah alone and set no other god beside Him. The relationship is mentioned to show that the messenger was not a stranger imposing an alien message. He belonged to the community he addressed. The same call to exclusive worship had been made through earlier prophets, so the demand was familiar rather than novel.

phrases.translation: proclaiming, “Worship Allah,” but they suddenly split into two opposing groups
phrases.explanation: The response to Salih's call was immediate division. The people became two quarrelling parties, one believing him and the other denying that he had been sent at all. The commentary explains the dispute as disagreement over his prophethood. The verse therefore introduces a pattern seen throughout the chapter, where a clear message does not produce unity but exposes the difference between faith and rejection within one community.

phrases.translation: He urged ˹the disbelieving group˺, “O my people! Why do you ˹seek to˺ hasten the torment rather than grace
phrases.explanation: Salih asks why his people seek to hasten punishment before mercy. The commentary explains the evil they demand as Allah's punishment and the good they neglect as mercy or well-being. Their urgency is misdirected, since they challenge the prophet to bring harm rather than seek relief. The question is a rebuke, but it also leaves a way out before judgment arrives.

phrases.translation: If only you sought Allah’s forgiveness so you may be shown mercy
phrases.explanation: Salih urges the disbelieving group to ask Allah's forgiveness so they may receive mercy. The commentary says this means repenting from unbelief, so Allah can forgive their great crime and remit the punishment they deserve. Mercy is not presented as unrelated to moral change. It comes through turning back to Allah, and the invitation shows that the threatened punishment was not yet irreversible.

phrases.translation: They replied, “You and your followers are a bad omen for us
phrases.explanation: The people claim that Salih and his followers are a bad omen, blaming them for expected calamities. The commentary connects this with practices of interpreting birds as signs of fortune. Their accusation shifts responsibility away from their own choices. Instead of answering the call to repentance, they treat the messenger and those with him as the source of whatever harm they fear.

phrases.translation: He responded, “Your omens are destined by Allah. In fact, you are ˹only˺ a people being tested
phrases.explanation: Salih replies that the reality of their omens rests with Allah, since no one knows whether suspected adversity or hoped-for good will occur. The commentary says their situation is a test through the sending of a messenger. Obedience brings a generous reward, while disobedience brings punishment. What appears to them as bad luck is therefore actually a moral trial in which their response determines the outcome.

phrases.translation: And there were in the city nine ˹elite˺ men who spread corruption in the land, never doing what is right
phrases.explanation: Nine men in the city of Thamud are singled out as corrupters who did nothing good. The commentary explains their corruption as disbelief and disobedience to Allah, and says all the disbelieving people shared in that corruption. These nine are named specifically because they plotted to hamstring the she-camel and conspired to kill Salih. Their wrongdoing is therefore active leadership in rejection, not merely private sin.

phrases.translation: They vowed, “Let us swear by Allah that we will take him and his family down by night
phrases.explanation: The nine conspirators bind one another with an oath to attack Salih and his family by night. The commentary says the Arabic wording can be read either as a command to swear or as a description of their swearing, with both readings accepted. Reports add that they hoped to kill him before the threatened punishment arrived. Their plan relies on secrecy, darkness, and mutual commitment.

phrases.translation: Then we will certainly say to his ˹closest˺ heirs
phrases.explanation: The plot includes a prepared statement to Salih's nearest relatives, who would be responsible for seeking justice. The conspirators intend to deceive those heirs about what happened, so the crime would appear unsolved. The commentary says the nine men were destroyed before they could carry out the attack. Their careful plan therefore fails at the first step, leaving only the divine response to it.

phrases.translation: We did not witness the murder of his family. We are definitely telling the truth
phrases.explanation: The conspirators plan to deny witnessing the murder and to insist that they are telling the truth. The commentary notes that this false claim would be made while Salih's family had in fact been destroyed. Reports describe angels striking the plotters with stones before they reached the prophet. Their intended lie never gets a hearing, because the punishment overtakes the liars before they can use it.

phrases.translation: And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware
phrases.explanation: The verse contrasts the secret plan of the conspirators with Allah's plan. The commentary explains Allah's planning as seizing wrongdoers suddenly while they are heedless, or leading them on until punishment strikes. Reports describe a boulder sealing the cave where the plotters waited. They thought they were acting unseen, but Allah knew their plan and acted with a knowledge they did not possess.

phrases.translation: See then what the consequences of their plan were
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to consider with the eye of the heart how the plotting of Thamud ended. The commentary says this reflection is also a warning to the Quraysh who reject Muhammad. Their denial places them in the same pattern as earlier peoples who opposed their messengers. The command turns a past destruction into present instruction, so the story is not merely historical information.

phrases.translation: We ˹utterly˺ destroyed them and their people all together
phrases.explanation: Allah destroyed the nine conspirators and the rest of Thamud together, leaving none of them alive. The commentary says this is the end of their treachery against Salih, and that the same divine custom applies to others who deny messengers and rebel. The collective destruction shows that the whole community bore responsibility, even though only nine men are named as the leaders of the plot.

phrases.translation: So their homes are there, ˹but completely˺ ruined because of their wrongdoing
phrases.explanation: The dwellings of Thamud remain empty and abandoned, with none of their former inhabitants left in them. The commentary says this ruin came because they wronged themselves by associating partners with Allah and denying His messenger. The homes are therefore not just archaeological remains. They are visible evidence of what their choices brought upon them, standing as a warning after the people have gone.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a lesson for people of knowledge
phrases.explanation: The ruin is called a sign or lesson for people who know. The commentary explains this as an admonition to those who understand what Allah did to Thamud, especially the Prophet's own people who were rejecting him. Knowledge here means recognizing the moral meaning of the event, not merely knowing that it happened. The sign calls its observers to draw the right conclusion before a similar fate arrives.

phrases.translation: And We delivered those who were faithful and were mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation: Allah saved Salih and those who believed with him from the punishment sent upon Thamud. The commentary describes their faith and affirmation of the messenger as the means by which they were spared. It also says Allah would similarly save Muhammad and his followers when punishment came upon the polytheists around them. Deliverance is therefore tied to belonging to the faithful community, while one report says they later settled in Palestine.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ Lot, when he rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people
phrases.explanation: The narrative turns to Lot, whom Allah sent to his own people. His rebuke is introduced as another example of a messenger confronting a community's settled wrongdoing. The commentary gives no extended introduction here because the story is already known. The phrase asks the reader to remember the moment of confrontation, when the prophet directly challenged what his people had come to treat as normal.

phrases.translation: Do you commit that shameful deed while you can see ˹one another˺
phrases.explanation: Lot asks how his people can commit the shameful act while seeing. The commentary explains seeing as knowing that the act is an abomination, especially since no earlier people had practiced it in that way. The wrong is therefore committed with awareness, not in ignorance of its novelty or ugliness. The phrase also suggests an open practice, since they see one another doing it rather than hiding it.

phrases.translation: Do you really lust after men instead of women
phrases.explanation: Lot names the specific disorder, that they approach men with desire instead of the women Allah made lawful through marriage. The commentary treats this as a reversal of what Allah permitted, not simply an excess of desire. The question is meant to expose the unreasonableness of their conduct. They have chosen a path that contradicts both the Creator's command and the lawful relations He provided.

phrases.translation: In fact, you are ˹only˺ a people acting ignorantly
phrases.explanation: Lot says they are a people acting ignorantly. The commentary explains this as folly and ignorance of Allah's great right over them, which leads them to defy His command and disobey His messenger. Their ignorance is not lack of information about the act's character, since the previous phrase says they understand it. It is a moral failure to recognize the authority of the One who forbids it.

phrases.translation: But his people’s only response was to say, “Expel Lot’s followers from your land
phrases.explanation: The people have no real answer to Lot's rebuke. Their only response is to call for the expulsion of Lot's household from the town. The commentary says they abandon argument and resort to removing the prophet and those associated with him. The demand shows that they experience his presence as a condemnation, even though he has only forbidden what Allah commanded him to forbid.

phrases.translation: They are a people who wish to remain chaste
phrases.explanation: They mock the followers of Lot as people who wish to remain pure. The commentary says this purity meant avoiding the shameful acts they practiced, and that the speakers reproached them without any fault. The accusation turns moral restraint into something contemptible. Their words reveal a community in which refusing wrongdoing is treated as grounds for exclusion rather than respect.

phrases.translation: So We delivered him and his family, except his wife
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Lot and the members of his household from the punishment, with one explicit exception. His wife is not included in the deliverance. The commentary gives no further detail about her action here, only that she is excluded by Allah's decree. The verse therefore separates the household into those rescued and one who remains behind, without turning the exception into a general judgment on families.

phrases.translation: We had destined her to be one of the doomed
phrases.explanation: The wife of Lot is described as one whom Allah had decreed to remain behind. The commentary explains the word as staying behind, not escaping with those who were saved. Her fate is presented as part of divine judgment, not as an accident of the rescue. The phrase preserves the seriousness of that decree while keeping the narrative focused on the deliverance of Lot and the punishment of his people.

phrases.translation: And We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺
phrases.explanation: Allah rains destruction upon the people, which the commentary identifies as stones of baked clay sent down from the sky. The translation calls it a rain of brimstone, but the emphasis is on a punishment that falls from above and overwhelms the town. The image turns something normally associated with mercy and life into an instrument of judgment, because the people had rejected the warning.

phrases.translation: How evil was the rain of those who had been warned
phrases.explanation: The rain is called evil for those who had been warned. The commentary says these people had been warned of Allah's punishment because of their disobedience and had been made to fear His power through the messenger sent to them. Their punishment is therefore not arbitrary. It comes after a clear warning, which makes the destructive rain the confirmation of the message they refused.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Praise be to Allah, and peace be upon the servants He has chosen
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to praise Allah for His favors, especially the guidance He has given, and to invoke peace on the servants He chose. The commentary understands peace as protection from the punishments that destroyed peoples like Thamud and Lot, and identifies the chosen servants with the companions and helpers of the Prophet. Praise and peace therefore come after stories of judgment, marking the safety granted to those who follow the messengers.

phrases.translation: ˹Ask the disbelievers,˺ “Which is better: Allah or whatever ˹gods˺ they associate ˹with Him˺
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether Allah or the partners associated with Him is better. The commentary explains the comparison in terms of worship and power. Allah has honored His friends and destroyed His enemies, while the idols can neither harm nor benefit themselves or their devotees. No reasonable person should confuse the two, yet the polytheists continue to mix worship of powerless objects with worship of the One who controls benefit and harm.

phrases.translation: Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who created the heavens and the earth, and sends down rain for you from the sky, by which We cause delightful gardens to grow
phrases.explanation: The argument begins with creation and provision. Allah created the heavens and earth and sends down rain, which may also include the springs He causes to flow from the earth. By that water He brings forth beautiful walled gardens, described by the commentators as orchards whose blossoms feed people and cattle. The verse moves from the vast structure of the cosmos to the food that grows within it, all dependent on His sending of water.

phrases.translation: You could never cause their trees to grow
phrases.explanation: The polytheists could not make the trees of those gardens grow. The commentary says that without the water Allah sends, they would have no power to produce the trees or prevent their growth, since such life cannot flourish without water. The phrase exposes the limits of human ability at a very ordinary point. People may cultivate and harvest, but the source of growth lies beyond their control.

phrases.translation: Was it another god besides Allah?” Absolutely not! But they are a people who set up equals ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: No other god has done the creating, sending of rain, or causing of gardens to grow, so the rhetorical question expects denial. The commentary says the polytheists set up equals to Allah knowingly, following the custom of their forefathers rather than lacking evidence. Their error is therefore a deliberate turning from truth. The question calls them back to what they already can observe in the world around them.

phrases.translation: Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who made the earth a place of settlement, caused rivers to flow through it
phrases.explanation: Allah made the earth a stable place of settlement where people can rest without it shaking beneath them, and He placed rivers within it. The commentary emphasizes both stability and flowing water as divine gifts. The question asks whether the idols, which bring neither benefit nor harm, are comparable to the One who prepared the ground for human life. The answer is assumed rather than stated because the evidence is immediate.

phrases.translation: placed firm mountains upon it, and set a barrier between ˹fresh and salt˺ bodies of water
phrases.explanation: Firm mountains are set upon the earth, and a barrier is placed between fresh and salt waters so that one does not spoil the other. The commentary understands the barrier as part of the order that makes the earth habitable. The verse groups mountains and separated waters with the earlier gifts of stable ground and rivers. Each detail points to a world arranged for life rather than left in chaos.

phrases.translation: Was it another god besides Allah?” Absolutely not! But most of them do not know
phrases.explanation: The denial of another god is followed by the statement that most people do not know. The commentary says they fail to understand Allah's greatness, the harm of associating partners with Him, and the benefit of sincere worship devoted to Him alone. Their ignorance concerns the meaning of the signs they live among. The verse therefore treats idolatry as a failure to recognize what creation plainly teaches.

phrases.translation: Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who responds to the distressed when they cry to Him, relieving ˹their˺ affliction
phrases.explanation: Allah answers the distressed person who calls on Him and removes the adversity that has afflicted him. The commentary explains the evil removed as hardship or calamity. The question contrasts this with the idols, who neither respond nor relieve. It appeals to the experience of need, when human beings discover their dependence and cry out to the One who can actually change their condition.

phrases.translation: and ˹Who˺ makes you successors in the earth? Is it another god besides Allah? Yet you are hardly mindful
phrases.explanation: Allah also makes generations of rulers and living people succeed one another on the earth. No other god bestows these favors, yet people remember them only a little. The commentary says this failure to reflect on Allah's greatness and benefits leads them to associate partners with Him. The verse closes the series of questions by tracing idolatry to forgetfulness rather than to a lack of signs.

phrases.translation: Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who guides you in the darkness of the land and sea, and sends the winds ushering in His mercy
phrases.explanation: Allah guides people through the darkness of land and sea, where darkness means losing the way on land or losing the path amid waves at sea. He also sends winds as glad tidings before His mercy, which the commentary explains as rain that revives dead land. The question joins guidance in danger with provision through rain. Both are ordinary experiences that point beyond human control.

phrases.translation: Is it another god besides Allah? Exalted is Allah above what they associate ˹with Him˺
phrases.explanation: No other god performs these acts, so Allah is exalted above the partners people assign to Him. The commentary explains exaltedness as elevation above both the association itself and the worship of anything beside Him. The rhetorical question assumes that guiding travelers and sending life-giving winds cannot be attributed to powerless idols. The verse therefore answers worship with a confession of divine transcendence.

phrases.translation: Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who originates the creation then resurrects it
phrases.explanation: Allah originates creation without any prior material, then causes it to perish and brings it back in the state it had before. The commentary stresses both the first act and the restoration, since the polytheists denied resurrection. The One able to begin existence can also renew it. The phrase therefore prepares the later argument that the Hour is not beyond the power of the Creator.

phrases.translation: and gives you provisions from the heavens and the earth? Is it another god besides Allah
phrases.explanation: Allah provides from the heavens and the earth by sending rain and bringing forth vegetation as food for people and livestock. The commentary again asks whether any god beside Allah does these things. The argument moves from the origin of life to its daily sustenance. Those who depend on rain and crops are living from a provision no idol has produced.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof, if what you say is true
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to demand proof from anyone who claims another god performs these acts. The commentary explains proof as an argument establishing the existence of such a partner. The challenge is not a request for rhetorical skill but for evidence commensurate with the claim. Since creation, resurrection, and provision all point to one source, the assertion of a rival remains unsupported.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “None in the heavens and the earth has knowledge of the unseen except Allah
phrases.explanation: The unseen belongs to Allah alone, and the Hour is included in what He has kept to Himself. The commentary says no inhabitant of the heavens or earth knows what Allah has reserved, and it preserves a report condemning anyone who claims to know tomorrow as inventing a lie against Allah. The verse sets a limit on all created knowledge, including that of prophets and angels.

phrases.translation: Nor do they know when they will be resurrected
phrases.explanation: Created beings also do not know when they will be raised from their graves. The commentary says this follows from the previous limitation, since the timing of resurrection belongs to the unseen. The denial is not about whether resurrection will happen but about knowledge of its moment. People may be warned that it is real while remaining unable to fix its date.

phrases.translation: No! Their knowledge of the Hereafter amounts to ignorance
phrases.explanation: The opening statement is explained through several accepted readings. One says the deniers' knowledge will catch up with the Hereafter only when they see it, too late for certainty to help. Another says their knowledge has gone astray and has not attained it at all. The commentary treats both main readings as sound. In either case, their present confidence about the Hour is without real knowledge.

phrases.translation: In fact, they are in doubt about it. In truth, they are ˹totally˺ blind to it
phrases.explanation: The verse then says they are in doubt about the Hour and blind to it. The commentary explains doubt as having no certainty that resurrection will occur, and blindness as lacking knowledge of when it will arrive. Their problem is therefore deeper than curiosity about a date. They neither accept the reality of the event nor grasp what has been told them about its coming.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers ask, “When we and our fathers are reduced to dust
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers frame resurrection as impossible by pointing to themselves and their ancestors becoming dust. The commentary says they imagine bodies decaying in graves and ask how such remains could be restored. The mention of fathers extends the objection across generations, suggesting that many have died without any visible return. Their question treats physical decay as the final fact.

phrases.translation: will we really be brought forth ˹alive˺
phrases.explanation: The challenge asks whether they will really be brought out alive in their former state after death and decay. The commentary understands the question as a denial of being raised from the graves. The verse does not answer with a philosophical argument here. It records the objection so that the following response can point to the ruins of earlier peoples and the limits of human knowledge.

phrases.translation: We have already been promised this, as well as our forefathers earlier
phrases.explanation: The deniers say the promise of resurrection was made to them and to their ancestors before, yet they have not seen it fulfilled. The commentary explains that earlier warners had already announced it, so the claim is not new to them. Their reasoning treats delay as disproof. Because generations have passed without the event, they assume it will never occur.

phrases.translation: This is nothing but ancient fables
phrases.explanation: They dismiss the promise as ancient fables, meaning fabricated stories written in old books and repeated without reality. The commentary says they regarded the teaching as something people had recorded, not as truth. This is a rejection of revelation's authority rather than a weighing of evidence. The label turns a warning about the future into folklore about the past.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the wicked
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to invite the deniers to travel and look at the dwellings of earlier peoples who rejected their messengers. The commentary says Allah destroyed those communities and left their homes empty, with traces and remnants effaced. The ruins are evidence of what denial brought. The instruction turns travel into reflection and warns that the same pattern could overtake the present audience.

phrases.translation: Do not grieve for them, nor be distressed by their schemes
phrases.explanation: Allah tells the Prophet not to grieve over the polytheists' rejection or be distressed by their plotting. The commentary explains this as comfort in the face of their denial and schemes, grounded in Allah's promise of victory over them. The command does not minimize the pain of opposition. It directs the Prophet to trust the outcome to Allah rather than be consumed by anxiety.

phrases.translation: They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass, if what you say is true
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers ask when the promised punishment will arrive if the believers are truthful. The commentary treats the question as a demand that the threat be fulfilled at once, mixed with doubt about the warning itself. Their wording challenges both the message and its messengers. Instead of repenting, they try to turn the promise into a test of credibility.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten is close at hand
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told that some of what they seek to hasten may already be near. The commentary explains the difficult verb as drawing near or being brought close, and identifies the near thing as a portion of Allah's punishment. The answer gives no date, but it reverses their mockery. What they treat as distant may have begun approaching them already.

phrases.translation: Surely your Lord is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most of them are ungrateful
phrases.explanation: Allah's bounty appears in His not hastening punishment on people for their disbelief and disobedience. The commentary says this patience is itself a favor, alongside many other gifts. Yet most people do not thank Him by devoting worship to Him alone. Instead they add to His worship things that harm them and cannot benefit them. Ingratitude is therefore shown not only in words but in misplaced worship.

phrases.translation: And surely your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal
phrases.explanation: Allah knows what people hide in their hearts and what they make public. The commentary says every concealed thought, secret intention, and open action is fully known and precisely accounted for. Nothing escapes His knowledge. This awareness leads to requital, since the doer of good will be repaid with good and the doer of evil with a fitting recompense. The verse therefore joins divine knowledge with moral accountability.

phrases.translation: For there is nothing hidden in the heavens or the earth without being ˹written˺ in a perfect Record
phrases.explanation: Nothing hidden in the heavens or the earth lies outside a clear Record. The commentary identifies this record as the Mother of the Scriptures, in which Allah has written everything that will occur from the beginning of creation until the Day of Resurrection. It is clear because it makes known to whoever reads it what Allah has recorded. The verse extends the previous statement about hidden hearts to all concealed realities.

phrases.translation: Indeed, this Quran clarifies for the Children of Israel most of what they differ over
phrases.explanation: The Quran tells the Children of Israel the truth about most matters in which they disagree. The commentary gives the dispute over Jesus as an example, where different communities made sharply conflicting claims and separated from one another. The Quran is presented as the arbiter of those disagreements. Its role is not merely to report the dispute but to tell the truth about it and guide people to the straight path.

phrases.translation: And it is truly a guide and mercy for the believers
phrases.explanation: The Quran is a guide and mercy for believers. The commentary explains guidance as Allah's clarification of the truth in religious matters people disputed, while mercy belongs to those who sincerely believe in it and act according to what it contains. The two gifts belong together. Clarification without response would not benefit, and claimed belief without action would not receive the mercy described here.

phrases.translation: Your Lord will certainly judge between them by His justice
phrases.explanation: Allah will judge between the differing parties among the Children of Israel. The commentary says His verdict will punish those in the wrong and reward those who act rightly and hold to the truth. The judgment is therefore not a vague settling of opinions but a moral decision. It brings the disputes mentioned in the previous verse to a conclusion based on justice rather than communal claim.

phrases.translation: for He is the Almighty, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: Allah is Almighty and All-Knowing in this judgment. The commentary explains might as His power to punish the wrongdoer, with no one able to restrain Him, and knowledge as His awareness of who is right and who has strayed. Justice is therefore supported by both power and knowledge. No party can escape His verdict, and no party can mislead Him about its true position.

phrases.translation: So put your trust in Allah, for you are surely upon the ˹Path of˺ clear truth
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to entrust his affair to Allah, because he stands upon clear truth. The commentary says this truth is evident to anyone who reflects with understanding, unlike the conflicting positions of the Children of Israel or the claims of the idolaters who deny him. The command also brings comfort. Rejection should not stop him from carrying out the mission Allah gave him.

phrases.translation: You certainly cannot make the dead hear ˹the truth˺
phrases.explanation: The dead here are not merely bodies in graves. The commentary interprets them as people whose hearts Allah has sealed, so they cannot comprehend the truth. The Prophet cannot make such a person understand, because Allah has decreed that he will not grasp it. The phrase uses physical death as an image of spiritual inability, emphasizing the limit of the messenger's power.

phrases.translation: Nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and walk away
phrases.explanation: The deaf are those whom Allah has made deaf to hearing the truth. The commentary says they turn away without listening, dominated by unbelief, so they neither reflect on the message nor pause to consider it. The Prophet cannot force a hearing on those who actively refuse it. The phrase therefore describes a moral refusal, not a physical disability, and warns against turning one's back on guidance.

phrases.translation: Nor can you lead the blind out of their misguidance
phrases.explanation: Two accepted readings describe the Prophet as not guiding those who are blind to the truth. The commentary says Allah has veiled their sight so they cannot discern the straight path, and that guidance belongs to Allah if He wills. The blindness is spiritual, not physical. It consists in being unable to see the way out of error, and the messenger cannot remove a veil that Allah has placed.

phrases.translation: You can make none hear ˹the truth˺ except those who believe in Our revelations, ˹fully˺ submitting ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The Prophet can make the truth heard only by those who believe in Allah's signs and submit to Him. The commentary explains signs as proofs, arguments, and revealed verses, and says true hearers listen, ponder, reflect, and act. Hearing is therefore more than receiving sounds. It is a response of faith and obedience, which is why the final phrase describes the receptive audience as submitted to Allah.

phrases.translation: And when the decree ˹of the Hour˺ comes to pass against them, We will bring forth for them a beast from the earth
phrases.explanation: When the decree of punishment takes effect against the deniers, Allah will bring forth a beast from the earth. The commentary explains the decree as wrath or punishment becoming due and links the sign to a time when people abandon commanding good and forbidding evil. It preserves many reports about the beast's appearance and location, but those details vary. The central point is a public sign after persistent rejection.

phrases.translation: telling them that the people had no sure faith in Our revelations
phrases.explanation: The mainstream reading says the beast speaks to people, while another reading says it brands them. The commentary accepts the widespread reading and explains the message as an announcement that people had no certainty in Allah's signs.
