It also notes two accepted recitations of the following clause. The sign therefore exposes the unbelief that preceded it, rather than offering a new opportunity to pretend certainty.

phrases.translation: ˹Watch for˺ the Day We will gather from every faith-community a group of those who denied Our revelations
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Resurrection Allah will gather from every generation and community a troop of those who denied His signs. The commentary explains signs as His proofs and arguments, and says a group from each community will be assembled. The phrase does not describe an indiscriminate crowd but the organized gathering of those defined by rejection. It marks the transition from warning to judgment.

phrases.translation: and they will be driven in ranks
phrases.explanation: The gathered deniers will be driven in ranks. The commentary says their foremost are held back until the stragglers catch up, just as guards order a crowd, and then they are driven toward the Fire. The image of ordered ranks reverses their earlier confidence. Those who refused to be guided in life are now controlled completely, gathered for the outcome of their denial.

phrases.translation: When they ˹finally˺ come before their Lord, He will ask ˹them˺
phrases.explanation: The gathered deniers are brought before their Lord, where they must answer for their rejection. The commentary says this happens after groups from every community have been assembled. The questioning is not for Allah to learn something new, since His knowledge has already been emphasized. It is a moment of accountability, when those who denied His proofs are made to confront the basis of their denial.

phrases.translation: Did you deny My revelations without ˹even˺ comprehending them? Or what ˹exactly˺ did you do
phrases.explanation: Allah asks whether they rejected His signs without comprehending them as they ought to have been known, and what exactly they had been doing. The commentary explains signs as proofs and arguments, and says the question concerns whether they denied or affirmed them. The rebuke exposes a refusal that was not grounded in real understanding. They had rejected revelation without first giving it the knowledge it deserved.

phrases.translation: And the decree ˹of torment˺ will be justified against them for their wrongdoing, leaving them speechless
phrases.explanation: The decree of punishment becomes binding on the deniers because of their wrongdoing. The commentary identifies that wrong as their denial of Allah's signs, and says His wrath is made obligatory for it. They are left speechless because they can offer no argument to avert the punishment that has overtaken them. The verse therefore completes the interrogation. Once judgment is established, excuses no longer have any effect.

phrases.translation: Do they not see that We made the night for them to rest in and the day bright
phrases.explanation: Allah points to the alternation of night and day. Night is made for rest, so bodies recover from the fatigue of daily activity, while day is made bright so people can see, move about, and seek their livelihood. The commentary says reflecting on this regular change should lead people to the One who can cause death and bring the dead back to life. The ordinary cycle becomes evidence for resurrection.

phrases.translation: Surely in this are signs for those who believe
phrases.explanation: The cycle of night and day contains signs for those who believe. The commentary says these signs confirm Allah's power over resurrection and His oneness. The change from darkness to light and back again is not difficult for the One who created both states, so restoring life after death is no harder. The signs are fully recognized only by those who already approach the world with faith.

phrases.translation: And ˹beware of˺ the Day the Trumpet will be blown
phrases.explanation: The Trumpet is described in the commentary as a horn or trumpet, with reports about a tremendous blast and an angel prepared to blow it. Another interpretation understands the blowing as being into the forms of creation. The reports contain many details, but the central point is a decisive sound that marks the Day. It announces the end of the present order and the beginning of judgment.

phrases.translation: and all those in the heavens and all those on the earth will be horrified ˹to the point of death˺
phrases.explanation: All in the heavens and the earth are seized with terror when the blast comes, except those Allah wills to spare. The commentary includes angels, jinn, humans, and devils among those overwhelmed, and reports identify the excepted group as martyrs who are alive with their Lord. The exception is real but not fully mapped out in the verse. Terror reaches the living creation while Allah preserves whom He chooses.

phrases.translation: except those Allah wills ˹to spare˺. And all will come before Him, fully humbled
phrases.explanation: Everyone will come before Allah in humility and abasement. The commentary explains the final word as disgraced or abased, and says the terrified cannot find any escape from Him. Two accepted readings of the verb give the same basic meaning. The verse therefore moves from the sound of the Trumpet and universal terror to the final gathering, where every creature stands low before its Lord.

phrases.translation: Now you see the mountains, thinking they are firmly fixed, but they are travelling ˹just˺ like clouds
phrases.explanation: People see the mountains and assume they are fixed, yet they are moving like clouds. The commentary explains that their great number can make swift motion appear stationary, like a vast army that seems still from a distance. The image belongs to the upheaval of the last day. What appears most solid and permanent is in fact being carried along by Allah's command.

phrases.translation: ˹That is˺ the design of Allah, Who has perfected everything. Surely He is All-Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: This motion is the design of Allah, who has perfected everything. The commentary says He made creation firm, beautiful, and even, and that He knows every good and evil act, every obedience and disobedience. He will repay each accordingly. The verse therefore joins the power displayed in creation with moral awareness. The One who orders the mountains also knows and judges human conduct.

phrases.translation: Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded with what is better
phrases.explanation: Whoever comes with a good deed receives something better. The commentary identifies the good deed especially with sincere monotheism and the confession that there is no god but Allah, and says the better reward is the Garden. Some interpreters clarify that nothing is better than faith itself, so the phrase means the good a person receives through it. The reward is therefore both a gift and the fruit of faith.

phrases.translation: and they will be secure from the horror on that Day
phrases.explanation: Such people will be secure from the terror of that Day. The commentary connects the terror with the blast into the Trumpet mentioned just before, and discusses two accepted recitations of the phrase. It prefers the reading that makes the terror definite, because that gives the fullest promise of safety from the horrors of the Day. The security is not from death but from the overwhelming fear of judgment.

phrases.translation: And whoever comes with an evil deed will be hurled face-first into the Fire
phrases.explanation: Whoever comes with an evil deed will be cast face-first into the Fire. The commentary repeatedly identifies the central evil deed here with associating partners with Allah, or disbelief, in contrast with sincere monotheism. The image is one of humiliation as well as punishment, since the face is thrown down. The verse sets the fate of rejection beside the safety promised to the faithful.

phrases.translation: Are you rewarded except for what you used to do
phrases.explanation: The final question asks whether they are repaid for anything other than what they used to do. The commentary says an implied statement is addressed to the polytheists after they are cast into the Fire. Their punishment corresponds to the deeds by which they provoked their Lord in worldly life. The question therefore denies arbitrary punishment and ties the outcome to their own persistent choices.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city ˹of Mecca˺, Who has made it sacred
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is commanded to worship the Lord of Mecca, the city Allah made sacred. The commentary lists protections associated with that sanctity, including against unlawful bloodshed, wronging others, hunting, and cutting its grass. Naming Mecca specifically reminds its people of Allah's favor toward them. The One who protected their city, rather than powerless idols, is the One they should worship.

phrases.translation: and to Him belongs everything. And I am commanded to be one of those who ˹fully˺ submit ˹to Him˺
phrases.explanation: To Allah belongs everything, and the Prophet is commanded to be among those who submit to Him. The commentary contrasts the Lord who owns all things with idols that own nothing, and says the command is to turn to Him with devoted religion. Submission here is not a private feeling alone. It is allegiance to the worship and way associated with the prophets, over against the religion of the idolaters.

phrases.translation: and to recite the Quran.” Then whoever chooses to be guided, it is only for their own good
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is also commanded to recite the Quran. Whoever follows that guidance benefits only his own soul, because faith and acceptance bring security from Allah's vengeance in this life and His punishment in the next. The commentary emphasizes that guidance is self-benefiting. The messenger's recitation does not need the audience's response for its own sake, since acceptance protects the one who accepts.

phrases.translation: But whoever chooses to stray, say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I am only a warner
phrases.explanation: Whoever rejects the message and strays is told that the Prophet is only a warner. The commentary says his task is to warn of Allah's punishment and wrath, to convey what he was commanded, and to offer sincere counsel. Acceptance brings good to the hearer, while rejection harms only the rejecter. The phrase defines the limits of prophetic responsibility without diminishing the seriousness of the warning.

phrases.translation: And say, “All praise is for Allah! He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to praise Allah, who guided him and his followers to the truth that the deniers could not see. He will show His signs so people recognize the truth of the warning. The commentary preserves two kinds of interpretation, signs of punishment and wrath, or signs in people themselves, the heavens, the earth, and provision. In both cases, recognition confirms the message they doubted.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation: Allah is never unaware of what people do. The commentary says an appointed term awaits the deniers, and when it arrives they can neither delay it nor bring it forward. The statement comforts the Prophet with the promise of victory and the humiliation of his enemies. Divine patience is therefore not neglect. Every deed is known, and the delay itself has a fixed limit.
